title: Two-stage decoder mediator: routing broker with acceptance thresholds and graceful fallback
creator: Avery Collins
description:
Goal: implement a two-stage "mediator" in the serving runtime that brokers between a fast 'draft' decoder and a more accurate 'final' decoder. The mediator evaluates draft tokens against configurable acceptance thresholds and decides whether to accept locally or forward to the final decoder. This enables aggressive latency reductions for friendly workloads while providing deterministic fallback to ensure output quality for high-risk inputs.

Scope: runtime changes to scheduling and routing logic, kernel selection guidance for both decoders, new lightweight acceptance scoring, metrics and fallbacks, and a minimal feature flag + config surface to tune thresholds per-route and per-customer. Exclude model training or model architecture changes; work assumes compatible model variants exist (e.g., smaller draft quantized variants + larger full-precision final).

Motivation: current decode pipeline either picks a single model (fast or accurate) or does ad-hoc speculative decode elsewhere. We need a first-class runtime component that: 1) orchestrates prefill+decode across two decoders, 2) applies deterministic acceptance checks cheaply, 3) falls back gracefully with clear latency and cost SLOs.

Success criteria: demonstrable p95 token-latency reduction for common chat prompts, <=1% increase in semantic regression (measured by eval prompts), clear cost savings for hosted workload, and no customer-visible production regressions during controlled rollouts.
acceptance_criteria: Mediator must route draft token streams and apply acceptance thresholds without blocking final decoder scheduling
Configurable per-route acceptance thresholds plus a global safe-mode override
End-to-end p95 token latency improvement >= 15% on chat benchmark A when mediator accepts >= 65% of tokens
When a token is rejected by the acceptance check, final decoder must produce a replacement token within fallback latency budget (configurable, default 120ms)
Instrumentation: token-level routing traces, acceptance decision logs, and a dashboard that shows accept_rate, fallback_rate, latency_p50/p95, and cost_delta
Feature-flagged rollout with canary and automatic rollback on quality regression (>1% MRR regression on eval set)
Automated integration tests simulating mixed workloads (short prompts, long context, multi-turn chat)
metrics: fallback_rate (fraction of tokens forwarded to final decoder)
decisions: Use lightweight token-level acceptance heuristics (matching probability delta + prefix-coherence score) instead of full LM-scoring to keep overhead low
Run draft decoder on same GPU as mediator when possible to avoid cross-device transfer for prefills
Prefer asynchronous final decoder scheduling with bounded waiting window rather than keeping request synchronous to the draft path
Expose per-route threshold config and emergency 'safe-mode' that disables acceptance and uses final decoder only
implementation_notes: Mediator will expose a small RPC between serving workers to hand off re-eval requests to final decoder instances
Acceptance checks must be vectorized over the token batch to avoid per-token kernel invocations
We will extend the kernel selection layer to expose a 'low-precision fast-mode' profile that optimizes for short-context draft decoding
KV cache handling: draft and final decoders must share compatible KV formats; if not available, mediator must trigger an efficient KV reconstruction for final decoder
Instrument the runtime to tag each token path (draft-accepted, draft-rejected, fallback-served) for tracing and billing
risks: Quality regressions if acceptance heuristics are too permissive — mitigated with conservative defaults and canary monitoring
Increased orchestration complexity could raise P99 latency tail in pathological workloads — mitigated by bounded waiting windows and backpressure to the draft path
KV cache incompatibilities between draft and final variants may force expensive cache rebuilds — need model onboarding checklist
Resource fragmentation: dedicating draft slots may reduce throughput under heavy load — evaluate autoscaling policies for draft pools
